title: Caching Common Development Dependencies
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of caching common development dependencies and identify when it should be used.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on caching common development dependencies. content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Cache keys should reflect package manager, OS/runtime, and dependency lockfiles so changed dependencies invalidate stale cached inputs. Artifacts preserve files produced by a run; caches accelerate reconstruction of dependencies. They serve different purposes and neither should contain secrets. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Compiled build caches
items.text: Cache rebuildable dependencies using a key that includes the package manager, runtime/OS as appropriate, and lockfile hash. A cache miss must not change build correctness, and secrets do not belong in caches.

content_blocks.code:
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
    with:
      node-version: "20"
      cache: npm
  - run: npm ci
  - run: npm test
content_blocks.expected_output: The setup action configures Node and dependency caching based on the npm lockfile; the tests still run even when there is a cache miss.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use this only in a Node project with a committed lockfile and test script. Review action source/pinning policy for production use.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain caching common development dependencies, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Choose between short-lived outputs, persisted artifacts, and reusable dependency caches.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Cache keys should reflect package manager, OS/runtime, and dependency lockfiles so changed dependencies invalidate stale cached inputs. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
